docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: This datasheet covers the technical information and design process of the IR proximity sensor control board.

docs.title: Project Summary
docs.text: This project will generate a haptic gripper to be mounted on a robotic system. The gripper will possess force sensors to detect the grip strength being used, motion sensors to detect any slippage, and an IR proximity sensor to detect and confirm that an object is in the claw. * The overall team report can be found here.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: This Block Diagram serves as an intial visualization of the final requirements of the circuit. The circuit runs on one main 5V power source, which the major components tie into as needed. The IR Emitter runs off the board's integrated PWM, and the IR Receiver feeds into an Analog to Digital Converter. The board connects to the main control hub through an eight-wire ribbon cable.

docs.text:
Infrared (IR) Emitter

  1. VSLY5940 Infrared Emitter

    • $1.56/each
    • link to product
    Pros Cons 10ns Rise/Fall Time 3 Degree Angle of Half Intensity Highest Radiant Intensity Most Expensive

  2. TSAL6400 Infrared Emitter

    • $0.52/each
    • Link to product
    Pros Cons 25 Degree Angle of Half Intensity Lowest Radiant Intensity Less Expensive Lower Max Voltage

  3. TSAL6100 Infrared Emitter

    • $0.52/each
    • Link to product
    Pros Cons 10 Degree Angle of Half Intensity Lower Radiant Intensity Less Expensive Lower Max Voltage

Choice: Option 2: TSAL6400 Infrared Emitter

Rationale: Given the intended short-range application, the greater Angle of Half Intensity provided by this option is more important than the lower radiant intensity. It is also one of the two cheaper options, with only a very small increase in the Rise/Fall times as a result. * The increased width of the beam will be beneficial for enableing easier reading of strangely reflective shapes, and the resulting loss of range is irrelevant in the current application * The Rise/Fall times of the compared Emitters are all very similar, and therefore did not contribute greatly to the decison.

Infrared (IR) Receiver

  1. TSSP4P38 IR Receiver

    • $1.99/each
    • link to product
    Pros Cons Greatest Receiving Distance Most Expensive Lowest Minimum Irradiance

  2. TSSP4056 Infrared Receiver

    • $1.36/each
    • Link to product
    Pros Cons Highest Maximum Irradiance More expensive Shorter Receiving Distance Highest Supply Current

  3. TSSP94038 IR Receiver

    • $1.08/each
    • Link to product
    Pros Cons Least Expensive Highest Maximum Irradiance Lowest Supply Voltage Shorter Receiving Distance

Choice: Option 2: TSSP4056 Infrared Receiver

Rationale: The three receivers are very similar in overall specifications, so the deciding factor was this receiver's greater maximum irradiance. Since this sensor will be used across relatively small distances, it will be helpful to have a better high range for more reflective objects closer to the sensor. * This sensor will be reading objects very close to the sensor, and therefore will be looking at brightly illuminated surfaces.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This schematic is design to support an Infrared Emitter paired to an IR Receiver, acting as a proximity sensor. The circuit runs on one main 9V power source, fed throgh a voltage regulator to 5 Volts which the major components tie into as needed. The IR Emitter (Vishay TSAL6400) runs off the board's integrated PWM, and the IR Receiver (Vishay TSSP4056) feeds into an Analog to Digital Converter through an Op-Amp (Microchip MCP6004) that strengthens the analog signal. The board connects to the main control hub through an eight-wire ribbon cable. Also included are two LED's and a swtich for debugging, as well as additional pin connections for additonal circuits or testing purposes.

Figure 1: The Schematic Itself.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: This Board needs to power the IR Emitter and Receiver, and while the majority of the components are relatively low in current draw, plotting the actual values ensures that the planned power source is adequate for the intended purpose.

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text: From the prepared Power Budget, the single 5V voltage regulator fed from external power will be adequate to supply the voltage and current the board.
